title: Making Inferences
presenterNotes: Use real polling data from news websites to show confidence intervals and margins of error in action.
Have students run a physical simulation: give each a die or coin to simulate sample proportions under a claim.
Emphasize that larger sample sizes narrow the margin of error, which is a key reason why major polls use samples of 1000+.

examples.prompt: A random sample of 40 teens has a total of 11,966 friends. Estimate the population mean number of friends $\mu$.
steps: Compute the sample mean: $ \bar{x} = \frac{11,966}{40} = 299.15 $.
The sample mean 299.15 is our best estimate of $ \mu $.
We estimate the average teen has about 299 friends.
examples.title: Example A – Estimating a Mean

examples.prompt: In a survey of 200 randomly selected city residents, 118 said they will vote for Candidate A. Estimate the proportion of all residents who will vote for Candidate A.
examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back...

Explain to a partner: Why is 118/200 a good estimate, but not exactly the true proportion? What would happen if we took another random sample of 200?
steps: The sample proportion $ \hat{p} = \frac{118}{200} = 0.59 $.
We estimate that 59% of all residents will vote for Candidate A.
Due to sampling variability, another sample might give 57% or 61%.
examples.title: Example B – Estimating a Proportion

examples.prompt: Four surveys about the incumbent class president show: n=10, 70%; n=20, 55%; n=30, 43.3%; n=40, 42.5%. Do you think the incumbent will be reelected?
examples.title: Example C – Class President Survey
steps: Small samples (n=10, 20) suggested the incumbent would win (>50%).
But larger, more reliable samples (n=30, 40) show support dropping to about 43%.
Since 43% < 50%, we predict the incumbent will likely not be reelected.

formulaCard.title: Point Estimates
notes: These are called point estimates because they give a single value.
Different samples give different estimates – this is sampling variability.

explanation: [[kw:Inferential statistics]] uses sample data to draw conclusions about a population. [[kw:Descriptive statistics]] only summarizes the sample itself.
A [[kw:sample mean]] ($ \bar{x} $) is the best estimate of the unknown [[kw:population mean]] ($ \mu $).
Formula for sample mean: $$ \bar{x} = \frac{\sum x}{n} $$
A [[kw:sample proportion]] ($ \hat{p} $) estimates the [[kw:population proportion]] ($p$). $$ \hat{p} = \frac{\text{number of successes}}{n} $$
[[imp:Larger sample sizes]] tend to give more accurate estimates because they reduce sampling variability.

blocks.title: Estimating Population Parameters

discoveryHook.scenario: You want to know the average number of friends a teen has on social media. Surveying every teen is impossible, but you can randomly survey a few hundred and use their average to estimate the true population mean. This is the essence of inferential statistics: using a sample to make a smart guess about a whole population!

confusionCorner.title: Small Samples Can Mislead

discoveryHook.scenario: A polling company claims 34% of adults say math is the most valuable subject. You survey 50 people and only 30% say math. Is the company wrong, or did you just get an unusual sample? A simulation can tell you how likely your result is if the claim were true!

questions.feedbackIfWrong: An extreme result suggests the claim is probably false.
questions.prompt: When a sample proportion falls in the far tail of a simulation distribution, the claimed population proportion is probably ___.
hints: Extreme results cast doubt on the claim.
The claim is likely not true.

questions.prompt: In a simulation of 100 samples assuming a claim is true, your sample result only appears 2 times. Is your result 'likely' or 'unlikely' under the claim?
hints: 2 out of 100 is a small percentage.
Compare to 5% or 10% benchmarks.

questions.prompt: A claim says p = 0.50. You simulate samples of size 50 and find 95% of sample proportions fall between 0.36 and 0.64. Your survey gives $\hat{p} = 0.66$. Is the claim plausible? (Answer 'yes' or 'no')
hints: Is 0.66 inside the interval 0.36 to 0.64?
If it's outside the 95% interval, it's suspicious.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: 0.66 is outside the typical range, so the claim is not plausible.

confusionCorner.body: Even if a sample proportion is extreme, the claim might still be true — you just got a very unusual sample. Statistics can never be 100% certain, but we can say a claim is 'probably' true or false.
confusionCorner.title: Rare ≠ Impossible

blocks.title: Analyzing a Claim with Simulation

explanation: A claimed population proportion is a hypothesis. To test it, we can run a simulation.
Steps: 1) Assume the claimed proportion is true. 2) Simulate many random samples of size $n$. 3) Record the sample proportion for each. 4) Build a dot plot or histogram.
If the actual sample proportion falls [[imp:in the tail]] (occurs very rarely), the claim is probably false.
If it falls [[imp:near the center]] (occurs often), the claim is plausible.
This method uses the variability of sample proportions to judge how extreme a result is.

rows.0: Near the center of the simulation distribution

rows.1: The claim is probably not accurate.

formulaCard.title: Using Simulation to Test a Claim
notes: The simulation models the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}$.
Typically, a result is 'extreme' if it occurs in less than 5% of simulated samples.
formulaCard.formula: $$ \text{If } \hat{p} \text{ is extreme under the claim } p_0 \text{, reject the claim.} $$

teacherCues: Remind students of hypothesis testing from 11.2. Ask: 'How can we tell if a sample result is unusual under a claimed population proportion?'
Show a dot plot from a simulation and ask where the sample proportion falls.

examples.title: Example A – 15 out of 50 Say Math
steps: The sample proportion is $ \hat{p} = 15/50 = 0.30 $.
In the simulation assuming the claim is true, 0.30 occurred 7/80 = 8.75% of the time.
This is not extremely rare; it can easily happen by chance.
Conclusion: The company's claim is probably accurate.
examples.prompt: Claim: 34% of adults say math is most valuable. You survey 50 randomly and find 15 (30%) say math. In a simulation, 30% occurred in 7 out of 80 random samples. What do you conclude?

examples.title: Example B – 25 out of 50 Say Math
steps: Sample proportion = 25/50 = 0.50.
In the simulation, 0.50 occurred only 1/80 = 1.25% of the time.
This is very unlikely if the true proportion were 0.34.
Conclusion: The company's claim is probably not accurate.

examples.prompt: Same claim (34%). Your survey of 50 finds 25 (50%) say math. The simulation shows 50% occurred in only 1 out of 80 samples. What do you conclude?

steps: 0.42 lies inside the 95% interval (0.20 to 0.48).
So this result is not unusual; it falls within the typical range of variation.
The company's claim is plausible.

blocks.title: Margin of Error

hints: Margin of error = 1 / √400.
questions.prompt: Find the margin of error for a survey with sample size n = 400. Answer as a decimal.

hints: Smaller sample → larger margin. So larger sample → ?
You can be more precise with more data.
questions.prompt: As the sample size increases, the margin of error ___.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: The margin of error decreases as sample size increases.

hints: Margin of error = 1/√2500 = 0.02.
Upper bound = 0.60 + 0.02 = ?

teacherCues: Ask: 'If a poll says 55% with a margin of error of ±3%, what could the true percentage be?'
Write the margin of error formula: ±1/√n. Show how it decreases as n increases.

discoveryHook.scenario: You hear that 60% of voters support a new law, with a margin of error of 4%. That means the true support is likely between 56% and 64%. The margin of error tells you how precise a survey result is — and it depends on the sample size!

confusionCorner.body: The formula $ \pm 1/\sqrt{n} $ works for sample proportions (percentages). For sample means, a different (and more complex) formula involving the standard deviation is used.
confusionCorner.title: Margin of Error Applies to Proportions

explanation: The [[kw:margin of error]] gives a range around a sample statistic that likely contains the true population parameter.
For a large population and a random sample of size $n$: $$ \text{Margin of error} = \pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} $$
This formula gives the margin of error for a [[imp:proportion]] at a 95% confidence level.
As sample size $n$ increases, the margin of error decreases. To cut the margin of error in half, you need to quadruple the sample size.
A confidence interval is calculated as: $$ \hat{p} \pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} $$

formulaCard.title: Margin of Error Formula
notes: For a proportion, expressed as a decimal. Multiply by 100 for percent.
Gives an interval that likely (95% confidence) contains the true population proportion.
Assumes a simple random sample from a large population.

examples.prompt: In a survey of 2048 people, 55% said TV is their main news source. Find the margin of error and the likely interval for the true percent.
examples.title: Example A – TV News Survey
steps: Margin of error = $ \pm 1/\sqrt{2048} \approx \pm 0.022 = \pm 2.2\% $.
We are confident the true population percent is between 52.8% and 57.2%.

Explain to a partner: Why does a smaller sample (1028 vs 2048) have a larger margin of error? How would the interval change if we surveyed 4000 people?
steps: Margin of error = $ \pm 1/\sqrt{1028} \approx \pm 0.031 = \pm 3.1\% $.
A larger sample would narrow this interval.

In a survey of 1020 U.S. adults, 41% said retirement is their top savings priority. Find the margin of error and the likely interval for the true percent.
steps: Margin of error = $ \pm 1/\sqrt{1020} \approx \pm 0.0313 = \pm 3.1\% $.
We estimate the true percentage is between 37.9% and 44.1%.

blocks.title: Interpreting Survey Results

confusionCorner.title: Don't Compare Overlapping Intervals Visually
confusionCorner.body: If two confidence intervals overlap, it doesn't necessarily mean the two proportions are not significantly different. Proper statistical tests are needed for comparison. However, for a single proportion against a benchmark like 50%, the interval method is fine.

teacherCues: Display a survey result: '52% approve, margin of error ±3%.' Ask: 'Can we be sure the majority approves?'
Explain that if the interval overlaps 50%, the result is too close to call.

discoveryHook.scenario: A poll says 52% of voters favor Candidate X with a margin of error of 3%. The interval is 49% to 55%. Since it includes 49% (below 50%), the race is still a toss-up! Understanding how to read a margin of error helps you separate a clear lead from a statistical tie.

steps: The entire interval is above 50%.
Yes, we can be confident the measure has majority support.
examples.prompt: A survey of 1600 voters finds 56% support a bond measure. Margin of error is ±2.5%. Does the measure likely have majority support?
examples.title: Example A – Clear Majority?

examples.prompt: A poll of 400 voters shows Candidate X with 51% support. Margin of error is ±5%. Should Candidate X feel confident?
examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back...

Explain to a partner: Why does 51% with a 5% margin of error not guarantee a win? What interval does this produce?
steps: Interval: 51% ± 5% = 46% to 56%.
This interval includes values below 50% (46%, 47%, etc.).
So the true support could be less than 50%. The race is too close to call.
examples.title: Example B – Too Close to Call

examples.prompt: Poll 1: n=500, 54% support. Poll 2: n=2000, 53% support. Which poll gives a narrower interval? Does the second poll's result show a clear majority?
examples.title: Example C – Comparing Two Polls
steps: Poll 1 margin: ±1/√500 ≈ 4.5%. Interval: 49.5%–58.5% (overlaps 50%).
Poll 2 margin: ±1/√2000 ≈ 2.2%. Interval: 50.8%–55.2% (entirely above 50%).
Poll 2 shows a clear majority; Poll 1 is too close to call.

explanation: A confidence interval gives a plausible range for the true population parameter.
If the interval for a candidate's support is entirely above 50%, we can be confident they are in the lead.
If the interval overlaps 50%, the race is too close to call – the candidate might actually have less than 50% support.
The margin of error also depends on the confidence level; $ \pm 1/\sqrt{n} $ gives about 95% confidence.

rows.3: Prop B might pass or fail (overlaps 50%)

formulaCard.formula: $$ \text{If interval is entirely above 0.5, majority is likely.} $$ $$ \text{If interval overlaps 0.5, too close to call.} $$
notes: An interval gives a range, not a single number.
Always check whether the margin of error changes the conclusion.
formulaCard.title: Confidence Interval Decision Rule

questions.prompt: In the inference blueprint, what is the first step? (Answer: Understand, Estimate, Quantify, or Conclude?)
hints: Starts with 'U'.
You identify the population and parameter here.
Starts with 'p'.
It's the unknown true value we are estimating.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: The margin of error gives a range for the population parameter.
questions.prompt: The margin of error gives a range that likely contains the true population ___.
A survey of 100 people finds 60% favor a new park. What is the margin of error? Answer as a decimal.
hints: That's 0.1.

rows.1: Compute $\bar{x}$ or $\hat{p}$ from the sample data.
Calculate margin of error = $ \pm 1/\sqrt{n} $; form interval.
Interpret the interval; decide if a claim is supported or if a threshold is met.

formulaCard.title: Inference Blueprint Formulas
notes: For proportions, use $ \pm 1/\sqrt{n} $ for the interval.
For means with large samples, a similar concept applies (using standard error).

explanation: 1. [[imp:Understand]] – What is the population and the parameter of interest (mean or proportion)? What does the sample tell us?
2. [[imp:Estimate]] – Calculate the sample mean $\bar{x}$ or sample proportion $\hat{p}$. This is your best single-number guess.
3. [[imp:Quantify Precision]] – Find the margin of error $ \pm 1/\sqrt{n} $. Construct a confidence interval.

4. [[imp:Conclude]] – Interpret the interval in context. Does it support a claim? Is it above/below a critical threshold? Acknowledge that the true parameter is likely in this interval, but not certain.

examples.title: Example A – Full Inference
steps: Understand: Population = all students at the school. Parameter = proportion $p$ who plan to attend college.
Estimate: $\hat{p} = 468/900 = 0.52$. So we estimate 52% plan to attend.
Quantify Precision: Margin of error = $ \pm 1/\sqrt{900} = \pm 1/30 \approx \pm 0.033 = \pm 3.3\%$. Interval: (48.7%, 55.3%).
Conclude: We are confident the true proportion is between 48.7% and 55.3%. Since this interval overlaps 50%, we cannot be certain that a majority plan to attend college.
examples.prompt: A survey of 900 randomly selected students finds that 468 plan to attend college. Make an inference about the proportion of all students at the school who plan to attend college.

steps: Estimate: $\hat{p} = 264/400 = 0.66$. Margin of error = $ \pm 1/\sqrt{400} = \pm 0.05$. Interval: (0.61, 0.71) or 61% to 71%.
The claim of 70% lies within our interval, so it's plausible. Our sample does not provide strong evidence against the company's claim.
If the interval had been (58%, 66%), 70% would be outside, suggesting the claim is too high.
examples.title: Example B – Testing a Claim
examples.prompt: A company claims 70% of customers are satisfied. You survey 400 customers and find 264 satisfied. Use the blueprint to evaluate the claim.
examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back...

Explain to a partner: How does the confidence interval help you evaluate the claim? What if the interval were (58%, 66%)?

examples.title: Example C – Election Prediction
examples.prompt: A poll of 1600 likely voters shows Candidate A with 55% support. Predict the election outcome using the inference blueprint.
steps: Estimate: $\hat{p} = 0.55$. Margin of error = $ \pm 1/\sqrt{1600} = \pm 0.025$.
Interval: 52.5% to 57.5%.
The entire interval is above 50%, so we can be confident Candidate A will win, barring major changes before the election.

teacherCues: Walk through a complete problem: 'A survey of 900 voters finds 54% support a candidate. What can we infer about the election?'
Use the steps: 1) Identify the parameter of interest. 2) Compute the point estimate. 3) Check simulation or compute margin of error. 4) Draw a conclusion.

confusionCorner.title: Confidence Interval Does Not Guarantee Truth
confusionCorner.body: A 95% confidence interval means that if we repeated the survey many times, about 95% of the intervals we construct would contain the true population parameter. We can't say there's a 95% chance that *this particular* interval contains the truth, but it's a standard way to express uncertainty.

discoveryHook.scenario: You've conducted a survey. How do you go from your sample percentage to a conclusion about the whole population? The Inference Blueprint guides you: estimate the parameter, gauge the precision with margin of error, and make a reasoned decision!
